newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, Dominican presidents discuss siege.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Dominican presidents discuss siege.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori on Sunday reportedly discussed possible asylum in the Dominican Republic for guerrillas holding 72 hostages in Lima, but said they would more likely be given refuge in a third country.

Fujimori flew to Santo Domingo for a lightning one-day visit and met President Leonel Fernandez for 3 1/2 hours to discuss a possible Dominican refuge for the guerrillas if there is a deal to peacefully end the crisis, a Dominican government source said.
"We are discussing that possibility but there is nothing concrete yet," the source said.
But, in a statement issued after the meeting, Fernandez's office said only that the presidents had touched on the hostage crisis.

"President Fujimori gave a brief explanation of the current situation of the talks between the Peruvian government negotiator and the representatives of the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement guerrillas)," the statement read.
It added that Fernandez told Fujimori of the Dominican experience in similar cases.
Fujimori said in a television interview broadcast on Sunday in Peru that the Dominican Republic would not be a likely destination for the rebels.
"I don't think the Dominican Republic will be acceptable to them (rebels) as a destination," Fujimori said.
"It's possible that in a third country at some moment it may be necessary and so we're talking about that in an informal way," he added.
He would not reveal the names of countries Peru has approached as possible refuges for the 20-odd rebels who have held captives including his brother Pedro in a diplomatic mansion for 75 days.

News reports have said Cuba, Nicaragua or Eastern Europe could be potential places of asylum in a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege. Fujimori said he has not spoken to Cuba's President Fidel Castro about asylum for the guerrillas.
After announcing his trip on late Saturday, Fujimori arrived in Santo Domingo on Sunday afternoon on a plane packed with reporters as well as his teenage son Kenji and a group of schoolmates.

It was his second visit to the Caribbean nation in less than a month, after he met Fernandez during a surprise four-hour stopover at Santo Domingo airport on Feb. 5 on his way back from a trip to Canada.
Peruvian government negotiator Domingo Palermo is due to meet the rebels for an eighth time in a Red Cross safehouse near the occupied Japanese ambassador's residence on Monday.

Officials left the seventh round of talks on Thursday in a relatively upbeat mood, and Fujimori spoke of a "rapprochement" between the two sides. But the guerrillas sent other signals on Saturday, unfurling defiant new banners promising no surrender.

The main Tupac Amaru demand is the release of 400 jailed comrades, but Fujimori has said the prisoners will stay where they are. The rebels are also demanding an improvement in extremely harsh jail conditions.

In Tokyo, the Japanese television network TV Asahi said Peru had decided not to press charges against one of its reporters and his interpreter for making an unauthorised entry into the diplomatic residence.
The Peruvian authorities had been considering charges of terrorism and treason against Tsuyoshi Hitomi, 27, a New York- based reporter for the commercial network, but decided there was no evidence.

The heavily-armed squad of Cuban-inspired guerrillas stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17. They swiftly freed hundreds of hostages but still hold two of Fujimori's relatives, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
